body_markdown:
If you’re the first person in your family to pursue education after high school, figuring out how to pay for career school can feel like learning a new language. FAFSA. Pell Grants. Aid offers. Student loans. Where are you even supposed to start?


Start with the FAFSA, then look into grants and scholarships before deciding whether you need to borrow. Career school students who attend eligible institutions may qualify for federal financial aid, providing more funding opportunities than you may realize. Here’s how to sort through them without assuming you already know how any of this works.


## 1. Start With the FAFSA


You’re going to hear this acronym a lot. FAFSA stands for Free Application for Federal Student Aid and filling it out is free.


The FAFSA is how you apply for federal student aid, including grants, work-study funds, and federal student loans. States, schools and some private organizations also use FAFSA information when deciding who qualifies for their financial aid programs. So even if you don’t think you will qualify for federal aid, it’s still important to fill out the FAFSA form.


Before you start, you’ll want to understand the process of[applying for federal aid through the FAFSA program](https://www.lincolntech.edu/news/skilled-trades/technology-and-skilled-trades/apply-fafsa-help-fund-trade-school-tuition) . That can be confusing when nobody in your family has done this before. Don’t guess your way through it. Federal Student Aid has instructions specifically for students and parents, and your school’s financial aid office can answer your questions.


## 2. See If You Qualify for Career School Grants


Grants are the funds you want to explore before you start thinking about loans.


The[Federal Pell Grant](https://studentaid.gov/articles/dont-miss-out-on-pell-grants/) is available to eligible undergraduate students with financial need, and unlike a loan, a Pell Grant generally does not need to be repaid. For the 2026–27 award year, the maximum Pell Grant is $7,395.


Pell Grants aren’t limited to four-year colleges. They can be used for school-related expenses at eligible career schools and[trade schools](https://www.lincolntech.edu/news/skilled-trades/technology-and-skilled-trades/what-trade-school-description-and-benefits) , as well as community colleges, online schools and four-year colleges and universities.


You may also come across state, school, or other grant programs. What you qualify for depends on your circumstances and where you plan to attend.


## 3. Apply for Career School Scholarships, Even the Smaller Ones


It’s easy to picture scholarships as giant awards with thousands of applicants. That’s only part of the picture. There are also plenty of[low-competition scholarships](https://www.sallie.com/resources/scholarships/lowest-competition) where your odds only improve if you apply. And there are[tips and tricks to help you navigate the scholarship process](https://studentaid.gov/articles/scholarship-tips/) .


To find potential scholarships, Federal Student Aid recommends checking with a school’s financial aid office, community organizations, local businesses, employers, state higher education agencies and organizations connected to your interests. Local scholarships can sometimes have smaller applicant pools. And make sure to check in with the career school itself. Some have scholarship and grant opportunities with different requirements depending on the program, campus, and applicant.


A $500 scholarship may not sound life-changing on its own. But several smaller awards can start knocking down what you need to cover yourself.


One other thing to remember: You should not have to pay someone to find scholarships for you. Watch out for scholarship scams and take advantage of the available free scholarship resources.


## 4. Figure Out What Trade School Will Really Cost You


Tuition is important, but it isn’t the only number you need. You may also need to budget for books, tools, transportation or other school-related expenses depending on your program. Then there’s the financial aid you receive, which can change how much you ultimately need to cover.


Comparing tuition prices alone can be misleading. Look at a school’s net cost, which accounts for scholarships and grants, when you compare your options.


Almost all schools have a[Net Price Calculator](https://www.lincolntech.edu/net-price-calculator) that can give you an estimate based on a selected campus. But it’s only an estimate, not a final financial aid offer.


Write the numbers down. Ask questions about anything you don’t understand. You’re not supposed to decode an aid offer from memory.


## 5. If You Borrow, Know What You’re Agreeing To


Sometimes grants and scholarships don’t cover the whole cost of attendance. That’s when loans may enter the conversation.


Loans, including federal student loans, are borrowed money that must be repaid. Your financial aid offer may include Direct Subsidized Loans or Direct Unsubsidized Loans. The main difference is that unsubsidized loans begin earning interest while you are still in school.


Before accepting a loan, look at how much you’re borrowing, the interest rate, and what repayment could look like. If you’re a first-time federal student loan borrower, you’ll also complete entrance counseling, which explains your responsibilities and the terms of the loan.


And just because you’re offered a significant amount of aid doesn’t mean you must accept every dollar offered to you. To be financially responsible, accept only what you truly need.


## 6. Use Your Career School’s Financial Aid Office


If your family has never dealt with financial aid before, you may not have someone at home who can explain what an aid offer means. That doesn’t mean you have to work through it alone.


Bring your questions to your school’s financial aid office. Ask what you qualify for. Ask what needs to be repaid. Ask what deadlines are coming up. If something doesn’t make sense, ask someone to explain it again.


Financial Aid representatives work with students to review possible funding options, and many schools offer federal financial aid assistance for those who qualify.


Being first means you’re doing something your family hasn’t done before. You don’t need to know the process before you begin.


If career training is your next step,[explore financial aid at Lincoln Tech and talk with a Financial Aid representative](https://www.lincolntech.edu/financial-assistance/how-do-i-apply) about the options that may be available to you.[Fill out the short form](https://www.lincolntech.edu/contact) to request more information and start planning how you can train—and pay—for a better future.
